Certain of Julien’s affection, perhaps her virtue would have found the strength to resist him. Trembling at the thought of losing him forever, her passion led her astray to the point of taking Julien’s hand again, which, in his distraction, he had left resting on the back of a chair. This action roused the young man’s ambition: he would have liked all those proud nobles to have witnessed it, those who, at table, when he sat at the lower end with the children, looked at him with such a patronizing smile. This woman can no longer despise me: in that case, he told himself, I must be sensitive to her beauty; I owe it to myself to become her lover! Such an idea would not have occurred to him before the guileless confidences his friend had shared with him.

The sudden resolution he had just made provided a pleasant distraction. He told himself: I must have one of these two women; he realized that he would have much preferred to court Mme Derville; not that she was more attractive, but she had always seen him as a tutor honored for his learning, and not as a carpenter’s workman, with a coarse woolen jacket folded under his arm, as he had appeared to Mme de Rênal.

It was precisely as a young workman, blushing up to the whites of his eyes, stopped at the door of the house and not daring to ring, that Mme de Rênal pictured him at his most charming. This woman, whom the local bourgeois called so haughty, rarely thought about rank, and the slightest certainty carried far more weight in her mind than the promise of character afforded by a man’s rank. A carter who had shown bravery would, in her mind, have been braver than a formidable captain of hussars adorned with his mustache and his pipe. She believed Julien’s soul nobler than those of all her cousins, all gentlemen of ancient lineage and several of them titled.

As he continued reviewing his position, Julien saw that he must not think of conquering Mme Derville, who was probably aware of the liking Mme de Rênal showed for him. Forced to return to the latter: What do I know of this woman’s character? Julien asked himself. Only this: before my journey, I took her hand and she withdrew it; today I withdraw my hand, and she seizes it and presses it. A fine opportunity to repay her for all the contempt she has shown me. God knows how many lovers she has had! Perhaps she decides in my favor only because of the ease with which we can meet.

Such, alas, is the misfortune of excessive civilization! At twenty, a young man’s education, if he has any education at all, is a thousand leagues removed from the freedom from constraint without which love is often merely the most tedious of duties.

I owe it all the more to myself, Julien’s petty vanity continued, to succeed with this woman, because if I ever make my fortune and someone reproaches me for the lowly employment of tutor, I shall be able to hint that love had cast me into that position. Julien once again drew his hand away from Mme de Rênal’s, then took hers again, pressing it. As they were returning to the drawing room, around midnight, Mme de Rênal said to him in a low voice:

“You will leave us, you will go away?”

Julien replied with a sigh:

“I really must go, for I love you passionately; it is a sin... and what a sin for a young priest!”

Mme de Rênal leaned upon his arm, and with such abandon that her cheek felt the warmth of Julien’s.

The nights of these two beings were very different. Mme de Rênal was exalted by the transports of the most elevated moral ecstasy. A coquettish young girl who begins loving early grows accustomed to the turmoil of love; when she reaches the age of true passion, the charm of novelty is lacking. As Mme de Rênal had never read novels, every nuance of her happiness was new to her. No sad truth came to chill her, not even the specter of the future. She saw herself as happy ten years hence as she was at that moment. Even the idea of virtue and of the fidelity she had sworn to M. de Rênal, which had troubled her a few days earlier, presented itself in vain; it was sent away like an unwelcome guest. I shall never grant Julien anything, Mme de Rênal told herself; from now on we shall live as we have lived for the past month. He will be a friend.




CHAPTER XIV

THE ENGLISH SCISSORS

    A sixteen-year-old girl had a rosy complexion,
    and she put on rouge.

    POLIDORI


For Julien, Fouqué’s offer had indeed deprived him of all happiness; he could not settle upon any course.

Alas! perhaps I lack character; I would have made a bad soldier of Napoleon. At least, he added, my little intrigue with the lady of the house will distract me for a while.

Fortunately for him, even in this minor, subordinate incident, the depths of his soul corresponded poorly to his cavalier language. He was afraid of Mme de Rênal because of her very pretty dress. In his eyes, that dress was the vanguard of Paris. His pride would leave nothing to chance or to the inspiration of the moment. On the basis of Fouqué’s confidences and the little he had read about love in his Bible, he devised a highly detailed plan of campaign. Since, without admitting it to himself, he was greatly troubled, he wrote this plan down.

The following morning in the drawing room, Mme de Rênal was alone with him for a moment:

“Have you no other name but Julien?” she asked him.

At this most flattering question, our hero did not know how to reply. This circumstance had not been foreseen in his plan. But for the folly of making a plan, Julien’s lively mind would have served him well; surprise would merely have added to the quickness of his perceptions.

He was awkward and exaggerated his awkwardness to himself. Mme de Rênal quickly forgave him for it. She saw in it the effect of a charming innocence. And precisely what she thought lacking in this man, whom everyone considered so gifted, was an air of innocence.

“Your little tutor inspires a great deal of mistrust in me,” Mme Derville sometimes told her. “I think he always has the air of thinking and of acting only with calculation. He is a sly one.”

Julien remained deeply humiliated by the misfortune of not having known how to reply to Mme de Rênal.

A man like me owes it to himself to make good this failure, and, seizing the moment when they were passing from one room to another, he believed it his duty to give Mme de Rênal a kiss.
